title: "My first weeks in MDS"
description: "Coming from GPU clusters to statistics, and what actually surprised me about the pace."

Orientation week was mostly logistics — accounts, laptops, a room full of people
introducing themselves — but the part that stuck with me was how quickly the cohort
stopped being strangers. Everyone had arrived from somewhere different: economics,
biology, public health, a few people coming back after years of work. I had half
expected a room of computer science graduates like me, and instead spent the week
being reminded that most of the interesting questions in this field arrive from
somewhere other than the code.

Then classes started, and the pace was the real surprise. I knew MDS was compressed;
I had not internalised what a block schedule feels like from the inside. A topic is
introduced, you use it in a lab two days later, and by the following week it is
assumed knowledge. Coming from a background where I would spend a week profiling a
single application before changing anything, the instinct to understand a thing
completely before starting stopped working almost immediately. What replaced it was
starting before I felt ready and letting the gaps show up in the error messages.

A few weeks in, I have settled somewhere between overwhelmed and genuinely enjoying
it. The tooling has been the easiest part to love — Git and the shell I already knew
from cluster work, and Quarto has quietly replaced a pile of habits I did not realise
were slowing me down; this site is a direct result. The statistics is where I am
working hardest, and that is exactly why I came. I spent my undergraduate years
making models run faster without being able to say much about whether their results
deserved the compute. That is the gap I am here to close. Ask me again after the
first round of quizzes.
